It did not "interpret the raw weights," it looked at the outputs of Qwen 0.8B and noticed that it was repeating itself in a loop, causing it to make trivial errors on a math test, even when it was capable of solving the problem. 

Astra then used standard interpretability techniques to isolate the neuron most responsible for this looping behavior, and ablate that looping behavior from the model by subtracting that direction from the activations. This suppressed the looping and allowed it to output the right answers.

This technique would not work on a model that did not have such a trivially suppressible issue. You cannot use a technique like this to make a normal model smarter at math.

Counterpoint on $MRVL / $LITE acqusition:

- "Every buyer that competes with Marvell will want a second, independent laser source".

They identify $SIVE / Scintil Photonics as new CW / ELS capacity, with names like $CRDO as potential partners of Sivers.

- "With Lumentum sold out for years, the overflow goes to whoever has merchant capacity"

Sivers was cited here, and comes online with 100M lasers / external foundry capacity (2:1 external/internal target). 

To demonstrate the sheer scale on that, $AAOI exit 2026 laser capacity target was roughly ~24M/year (but different blend). 

- "Module makers move upstream" was also another second order effect. 

 $JBL as one example is now heavily competing with the combined Lumentum + Marvell.... There's other players like $SMTC that are explicitly doing M&A for expanding laser capacity.

I don't think the overall AI valuation crash is representative of individual company strength in the optical sector.

There's very compelling opportunities in the laser bottleneck in the upcoming year that I believe markets are mispricing.

everyone believes intelligence has unlimited demand, not just the maxis. but what the maxis get wrong is that the intelligence anthropic and openai and frontier models are building isn’t the generic kind you’re picturing. let me explain-

the two biggest uses of compute are crudely either training or inference. the “generic intelligence” everyone says has unlimited demand comes from mainly inference, and inference needs very different power and utilization than training. inference comes in bursts, so you have to by default overbuild capacity to handle the peaks until the utilization problem is solved, which means almost by definition we are going to overbuild. but training doesn’t have that problem: the workload is steady and the demand curve is knowable. so data centers end up overbuilt right now precisely because utilization isn’t optimized yet.

so anthropic and the other frontier labs are building their future on training, which is why they are saying they can soak up all this excess capacity. but their “intelligence” isn’t workplace productivity. it’s the leap toward singularity-type outcomes: new drug discoveries, cyber capabilities, recursive self-improvement. these are true 1-of-1s. that’s why when anthropic talks about “existential threats to humanity,” it isn’t talking about job losses, not really. it’s saying they’re on the precipice of unbelievable discoveries, because they’re still TRAINING MORE MODELS.

but distillation is real and open source is real. the half-life of any frontier model is tiny because nothing protects it the way IP protects a patent. imagine a rare disease drug company that spends billions on research, and two months after a breakthrough a generic shows up. that company can never recoup its investment, unless it can discover an infinite number of rare disease drugs. THAT is the kind of intelligence anthropic is betting on. that’s what the $800bn of compute spend is betting on.

so the questions you need to ask are: 1) if intelligence is two-tiered, what does each tier cost? what’s the cost of AGI, and what’s the cost of the generic intelligence that has infinite demand? and 2) are we allocating capital with the right risk curve and decay function to find out whether the AGI payoff is real? and if it is real, could a private company ever truly own it?

that’s the cognitive dissonance at the heart of this entire paradox: everyone is gaslighting each other about what intelligence is as the unit of measurement is purposely kept vague by both the users and the suppliers. generic intelligence has unlimited demand, but it’s a certain race to the bottom. "superintelligence" is the opposite: it can't have unlimited demand by definition, but if it delivers even half of what it promises, no private company will ever get to keep it, at least not without the government stepping in to guard the moat (which is why anthropic keeps playing this angle up, without having shown any demonstration they are near this level of discovery at all). and at that point you have to ask who is going to hold the bag, and whether that was in fact, very intelligent at all.

$PLTR 

Palantir, once again, puts up one of the best quarters that the market has ever seen.

Being able to grow revenues 96% while having 62% adjusted operating income margins is unheard of. There is no other software company that is even close to putting up these types of results.

US commercial revenue officially passed US government revenue for the first time. I remember in 2022, the bear case was centered around the company being too reliant on the USG. If anything, that was the bull case because that gave them the time to figure out how to scale US commercial and now we have a company doing 29% growth QoQ, which would be amazing YoY for most companies as Dr. Karp said, but also scaling that YoY growth at 148% for US commercial. 

It is unprecedented. 

So, why? Why is it happening? 

Well, it seems like Sovereignty is a very, very big deal.

“The Sovereign AI movement is imposing the most dramatic dichotomy between haves and have nots that I have witnessed in 30 years of business. Every institution—government and commercial—is rapidly being forced, voluntarily or not, into one of these two categories,” said Alex Karp.

Having been to multiple AIPCons and Institutional Sovereignty bootcamps this year, I can say that this is very real. When you talk to customers, you realize that they want much, much more than just plugging their enterprise into an LLM. They actually want FDEs, they want the grunt work of figuring out how to build custom workflows, they want the post training and fine tuning of open models...they want outcomes. The reason Palantir is growing this fast and continuing to show so much operating leverage is because they are delivering outcomes. That's why this is working. 

The company is doing this with 1090 customers. Most enterprise software companies at this scale have well over 100K customers. I mean, once again, this is unprecedented. Their net dollar retention scaled to 165%...their rule of 40 is now a new record at 158%...these are numbers that you only get when the company's entire mission is geared towards making sure their partners succeed and as a result, they are being paid for that value and then monetizing that value at the highest efficiency any software company ever has before with these margins. 

Stock is down due to macro, midterms, etc. but the core business is growing faster than anything we have ever seen and doing so in one of the most profitable ways ever. Their adjusted FCF in 90 days is now equal to the revenue they were bringing in early last year. 

An incredible quarter by Palantir, congrats to all shareholders and a deep thank you to the executive team and employees.

A TON OF THINGS HAPPENED IN THE STOCK MARKET TODAY.

Here's a full recap:

1. Palantir $PLTR delivered an extraordinary Q3 2026, with revenue surging 96% YoY to a record $2.31B, marking its first quarter above $2B, while U.S. commercial revenue skyrocketed 148% YoY to $984M, surpassing U.S. government revenue of $953M for the first time in company history. Total U.S. revenue grew 119% to $1.94B, while adjusted EPS reached $0.44 and GAAP net income climbed to $1.13B. Profitability remained exceptional, with adjusted operating income of $1.43B, representing a 62% margin, and adjusted free cash flow of $1.22B, representing a 53% margin. Palantir achieved a remarkable Rule of 40 score of 158%, closed 64 deals worth at least $10M, and grew U.S. commercial remaining deal value 79% YoY to $6.52B. Management also significantly raised FY2026 revenue guidance to $8.53B, representing 91% annual growth, while projecting U.S. commercial revenue growth of at least 143% and adjusted free cash flow of $4.8B–$5B. CEO Alex Karp emphasized that the accelerating sovereign AI movement is creating unprecedented demand for Palantir's AIP, Foundry, and Ontology platforms, as governments and enterprises increasingly seek to deploy AI using their own proprietary data and infrastructure.

2. Meta $META and Oracle $ORCL are preparing major capital raises as the world's largest technology companies continue securing funding for their expanding AI infrastructure investments. Meta is reportedly targeting at least $20B through a U.S. dollar- and euro-denominated bond offering, potentially spanning five dollar tranches and six euro tranches, with Citigroup $C and Morgan Stanley $MS coordinating investor calls. Meanwhile, Oracle is reportedly preparing a nearly $10B equity offering at an approximately 11% discount, alongside a six-part U.S. dollar investment-grade bond offering and a newly filed mixed shelf registration. Fitch estimates Oracle's combined capital raise at approximately $20B, including $10B in equity. 

3. Grab $GRAB delivered strong Q3 2026 results, with revenue increasing 27% YoY to $1.11B and adjusted EBITDA surging 73% to a record $237M, while its adjusted EBITDA margin expanded 565 basis points to 21.3%. Monthly transacting users reached a record 57.2M, up 20% YoY, as Grab added 3.3M users during the quarter, its strongest quarterly addition since Q1 2022. On-Demand GMV grew 18% to $6.84B, while Financial Services revenue surged 124% to $201M, with the segment achieving adjusted EBITDA profitability for the first time at $12M. Grab also raised its FY2026 revenue guidance to $4.15B–$4.20B and adjusted EBITDA outlook to $790M–$800M, reflecting accelerating profitability across its ecosystem. The company generated $286M in quarterly adjusted free cash flow, repurchased $400M in shares during September and October, and retains another $500M in buyback authorization, highlighting improving operating leverage and increasing shareholder returns. 

4. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance expressed growing optimism about a potential U.S.–Iran agreement, with Vance saying he feels “good about the prospects” of a deal following several productive discussions with Iranian officials. Vance confirmed that no deadline has been established for resuming military strikes, while Trump said negotiations are “coming together nicely” and suggested that progress toward an agreement has contributed to falling oil prices. Trump also said Iran wants to reach a deal, reiterated Tehran's assurances that it would not develop nuclear weapons, and indicated that the U.S. would refrain from further strikes against Iranian leadership. Meanwhile, Qatari mediators are reportedly traveling to Tehran to meet Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and discuss a revised agreement that has been under negotiation for eight days, according to Reuters. However, Iranian state-linked Fars News pushed back against reports of a breakthrough, citing a source who said no meaningful progress has occurred and that Tehran will not move forward until Washington satisfies Iran's seven conditions. 

5. The top 10 most active options today by contracts traded were $NVDA with 4.7M contracts, $TSLA with 3.7M contracts, $INTC with 2.1M contracts, $MU with 1.8M contracts, $AMZN with 1.8M contracts, $AAPL with 1.6M contracts, $GOOGL with 1.0M contracts, $AMD with 1.0M contracts, $SPCX with 1.0M contracts, and $ORCL with 768K contracts.

6. Anthropic is reportedly facing pressure from institutional investors to price its upcoming November IPO at a $1.5T–$1.6T valuation, down from earlier expectations approaching $2T, according to the Wall Street Journal. The more cautious outlook follows the recent technology selloff and growing concerns over the sustainability of massive AI infrastructure spending, despite Anthropic reporting $17B in Q3 revenue, up from $11.6B in Q2, even after approximately $600M in pricing reductions and customer discounts. The company has also disclosed an extraordinary $895.4B in combined AI computing purchase and lease commitments, including $447.5B expected before 2031, with most remaining obligations extending through 2045. Anthropic could begin its IPO roadshow next week, with trading potentially starting before Thanksgiving, although the final valuation, offering size, and share price remain undetermined. 

7. Marvell $MRVL announced a massive $115B all-stock acquisition of Lumentum $LITE, creating a new powerhouse in AI networking, optical connectivity, and custom silicon. Under the agreement, Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share, valuing Lumentum at approximately $1,132 per share, a 23.9% premium to its unaffected closing price. Following the transaction, Marvell shareholders will own 67% of the combined company, with Lumentum shareholders owning 33%. The merger combines Marvell's expertise in custom AI chips, switching, and electrical interconnects with Lumentum's leadership in lasers, optical transceivers, and optical circuit switching, positioning the combined business to address an estimated $550B total addressable market. 

8. U.S. equity funds recorded $6.7B in net outflows during the week ending October 28, marking their largest weekly withdrawal since mid-September and reversing the $5.1B and $13B in inflows recorded over the previous two weeks. Meanwhile, global equity funds attracted $10.2B, extending their inflow streak to six consecutive weeks, although demand slowed considerably from $25.1B and $19.8B in the preceding weeks. Asian equity funds led global inflows with $9.9B, down from $11.6B the prior week, while European equity funds attracted another $4.5B. 

9. Disney $DIS is reportedly preparing to eliminate thousands of jobs as part of a major cost-cutting initiative, with some managers instructed to target 20% in annual cost savings across their operations. The reductions are expected to come from a combination of workforce layoffs and lower operating expenses, with certain business divisions facing deeper cuts than others. Disney, which employed approximately 231,000 people worldwide at the end of its last fiscal year, plans to redirect a portion of the savings toward film and television programming, technology, theme parks, and cruise operations. 

10. Bloom Energy $BE and California Resources Corporation $CRC signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding to explore the development of more than 1 GW of power generation capacity in California, combining Bloom's solid-oxide fuel cell technology with carbon capture and storage infrastructure. Under the proposed partnership, Bloom would provide its on-site power generation systems, while CRC's Carbon TerraVault would handle CO2 transportation and permanent underground storage. The projects, being evaluated across Central and Northern California, could supply electricity to AI data centers, utilities, and industrial customers, with the companies estimating that up to 3 million metric tons of CO2 annually could be available for capture and storage. 

11. AST SpaceMobile $ASTS and AT&T $T announced the first successful handoff of an active cellular connection between a terrestrial network and a satellite network using an unmodified smartphone, marking a significant milestone for direct-to-device satellite connectivity. The test successfully transferred an active connection between AT&T's ground-based cellular infrastructure and AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird satellites, leveraging networking technology from Ericsson $ERIC and Nokia $NOK. The achievement demonstrates progress toward enabling ordinary smartphones to transition between traditional cell towers and satellite coverage without requiring specialized hardware. AT&T said the next step will involve real-world beta testing ahead of a potential commercial rollout, bringing AST SpaceMobile closer to delivering satellite-based cellular coverage in areas where conventional networks are unavailable.

12. Piper Sandler believes a potential SpaceX $SPCX and Tesla $TSLA merger proposal is now more likely than not, as both companies have reportedly established independent special committees to evaluate a possible combination. The firm expects Elon Musk to retain more than 70% voting control of the combined entity under most potential transaction structures, allowing him to maintain significant influence over the businesses. A merger could bring together Tesla's electric vehicles, autonomous driving, robotics, and energy infrastructure with SpaceX's satellite connectivity, launch operations, and AI computing capabilities, potentially creating one of the world's most vertically integrated technology companies.
